candidates.statement: This guidance is intended to facilitate progress in the field of pharmacogenomics and the use of 16 pharmacogenomic data in drug 2 development. This document is intended to clarify the contexts 17 in which pharmacogenomic study findings and data must be included in submissions related to 18 investigational new drug applications (INDs), new drug applications (NDAs), and biologics 19 license applications (BLAs) based on the FDA’s regulations. In addition, this document provides 20 recommendations to sponsors and applicants on the format and content of the pharmacogenomic 21 data submissions. 22
candidates.context: For the purposes of this guidance, the term pharmacogenomics is defined as the study of 24 variations of DNA and RNA characteristics as related to drug response; 3 DNA or RNA 25 variations can be germline, somatic, or microbial. Pharmacogenomics does not refer to data 26 resulting from proteomic, metabolomic, or other -omic studies, although similar considerations in 27 this guidance could be applicable for determining whether to submit findings and data from such 28 studies. 29

candidates.statement: Sponsors and applicants submitting or holding INDs, NDAs, or BLAs are subject to FDA 49 requirements for submitting data to the FDA that are relevant to drug safety and effectiveness. 4 50 However, the regulations were developed before the advent of widespread animal or human 51 genetic testing (e.g., high-throughput DNA sequencing) or gene expression testing and do not 52 specifically describe the submission requirements for such data as a separate category. 5 53
candidates.context: Pharmacogenomic studies have the potential to help identify sources of interindividual 43 variability in drug exposure or response (both effectiveness and toxicity), making it possible to 44 optimize therapy for individuals. Currently, several pharmacogenomic biomarkers with well- 45 accepted mechanistic and clinical significance are being integrated into drug development (e.g., 46 enriched clinical trial designs) and clinical practice. 47 This guidance, when final, will constitute the FDA's current thinking about pharmacogenomic 55 study results and the associated data required to be submitted in IND, NDA, or BLA 56 submissions, as well as the FDA’s recommendations as to the level of detail and format for 57 reporting. candidates.statement: The FDA’s regulations establish requirements for the submission of information in INDs, NDAs, 68 and BLAs. 7 Consistent with these regulations, the sections below summarize the contexts in 69 which pharmacogenomic study results and data must be reported in IND, NDA, and BLA 70 submissions. 8 71

Table 1 also summarizes the FDA’s recommendations on the amount and level of detail to report 73 for each context in which pharmacogenomic study results and data are reported to the FDA. The 74 amount and level of detail to report to the FDA should vary depending on the context of how the 75 genomic biomarkers are utilized and the potential risks associated with the biomarker. For 76 example, data related to exploratory safety studies should be supplied in a brief synopsis, 77 whereas data supporting statements in FDA labeling should be supplied in submission of subject- 78 level data from clinical trials. Genomic data that fit multiple contexts should be submitted at the 79 more detailed reporting level. For example, genomic biomarker studies that are related to 80 pharmacokinetics (e.g., drug metabolizing enzyme gene variants) are recommended to be 81 submitted as a synopsis. However, if those same genomic data are also the basis for patient 82 dosing, subject-level data, and a full report rather than only a synopsis should be submitted. 83 More detailed reports and data can be submitted where synopses are recommended. Furthermore, 84 the FDA may request additional data (e.g., detailed reports, subject level data) as needed for the 85 review of IND submissions as well as NDAs or BLAs as outlined in 21 CFR parts 312, 314, and 86

candidates.statement: • 21 CFR 314.50 outlines the NDA submission requirements. As the introduction to 21 176 CFR 314.50 states, “[t]he NDA is required to contain reports of all investigations of the 177 drug product sponsored by the applicant, and all other information about the drug 178 pertinent to an evaluation of the NDA that is received or otherwise obtained by the 179 applicant from any source.” Information that is pertinent to an evaluation of the 180 application includes information related to each controlled clinical study pertinent to a 181 proposed use of the drug, a description and analysis of “any other data or information 182 relevant to an evaluation of the safety and effectiveness of the drug product,” and “[a] 183 summary and updates of safety information.” 24 The pharmacogenomic studies required to 184 be submitted to the FDA for an IND are generally relevant to the FDA’s evaluation of the 185 safety and effectiveness of a drug product. Therefore, to comply with these regulations, 186 sponsors must provide reports of certain pharmacogenomic studies in their NDAs as 187 outlined in Table 1. 25 Table 1 also specifies the recommended reporting level for each 188 type of pharmacogenomic study reported in NDAs. Sponsors can discuss submission of 189 pharmacogenomic reports and data in NDA submissions at pre-NDA meetings. 190

candidates.statement: • In addition, if a sponsor intends for pharmacogenomic study data to be used in the drug 203 labeling or as part of the scientific database being relied upon to support approval, then 204 data must be submitted from such studies to the NDA or BLA. 27 Such data should be 205 submitted as subject-level data in a detailed report. This includes data pertaining to 206 pharmacogenomic biomarkers that inform labeling, because the data pertain to selecting 207 patients for clinical trials (whether enrollment is limited to or stratified by the 208 biomarkers), determining dosing and administration, or informing drug-drug interactions 209 (or lack thereof). Also, information not tied to specific clinical recommendations must be 210 submitted if it relates to any narrative about the drug’s pharmacokinetic disposition or 211 clinical trial populations in labeling. 28 212
